analogy.p: Lady Macbeth is like a thermostat set to its highest level to keep a room hot: she has to run constantly to maintain the temperature of Macbeth's ambition. For a while the room is warm, but the effort wears the machine out, and when it fails the whole system overheats. The analogy captures how her toughness is a performance that costs her heavily. It breaks down because a thermostat has no conscience to rebel against the setting.

bullets: **Function**: she is the human instrument of temptation, more immediate than the supernatural witches.
**Role in the structure**: she dominates Act 1 and the murder in Act 2, fades in Act 3, and returns only for the sleepwalking scene (5.1). Her absence from Act 4 mirrors her loss of influence.
**Dramatic mirror**: her decline in Act 5 parallels, and ironically reverses, Macbeth's rise: he grows harder as she becomes more vulnerable.
**Interpretations differ**: she is a manipulative “fiend-like queen” (Malcolm's phrase, 5.8), a woman limited by the options of her time, or a person who underestimates her own conscience.

callouts.p: A foil is a character who contrasts with another in order to highlight qualities. Lady Macbeth acts as a foil to Macbeth because she seems decisive when he hesitates, but the roles swap by Act 3.
Examiners reward answers that see her as complex: persuasive and ruthless, but also unable to kill Duncan herself and ultimately broken by guilt.
callouts.t: She is not a simple villain

core.h: Who she is and what she does in the play
core.p: Lady Macbeth is the character who turns Macbeth's private ambition into action. She appears first in 1.5, reading her husband's letter about the witches, and within a few lines she has already decided that Duncan must die. Her speeches show a quick, strategic mind and a talent for words that persuades Macbeth where the witches could only tempt him. Yet by Act 5 she is reduced to a sleepwalker, haunted by the very blood she once thought could be washed away with “a little water”.

bullets: **“Unsex me here”**: she asks to lose female nature (compassion, maternity) in order to commit murder. The imperative form shows that she gives orders to the spirits, not requests.
**“Take my milk for gall”**: milk, the symbol of nurture, is to be replaced by gall, a bitter poison. The image reverses motherhood into destruction.
**“Come, thick night”**: she asks for darkness to hide the deed from heaven. The same imagery appears in Macbeth's “stars, hide your fires”, linking them as conspirators.
**“Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't”**: the advice to hide wickedness beneath a pleasant face echoes the garden of Eden, associating her with the serpent.
**Syntax of command**: the sentences are full of imperatives (“come”, “take”, “pour”) which show how she sees action as a matter of will.

callouts.p: Choose “unsex me here” and write about the verb “unsex”: it suggests removing something innate, and the casual “here” makes the demand feel immediate, as if she expects the spirits to respond on the spot. Then say what this shows about her view of women and power.

core.h: Act 1 Scene 5: the invocation of evil
core.p: Her first soliloquy is among the most striking in the play because she rejects her own femininity in order to murder. She fears that Macbeth is “too full o' th' milk of human kindness” to take the “nearest way”, and she resolves to “pour my spirits in thine ear” so that she can remove the obstacles to his ambition. Her language moves quickly from analysis to invocation as she calls on dark spirits to help her.

bullets: Her argument uses **emotional blackmail** more than logic; she never answers his moral reasons, only questions his courage.
The baby image (“I have given suck”) suggests she has been a mother; critics debate whether this means a lost child or is a rhetorical exaggeration.
By the end of the scene Macbeth is describing her as someone who should only “bring forth men-children”, a reversal of the earlier doubt.
Notice the **power balance**: Macbeth's hesitation is expressed in long soliloquy; she speaks in short, decisive sentences.

callouts.p: In Jacobean England women had limited public power, so she can only act through her husband. Her language of “manhood” shows that she believes power belongs to men and that she must borrow it.

core.p: When Macbeth says “We will proceed no further in this business”, Lady Macbeth uses a series of rhetorical strategies to reverse his decision. She attacks his courage (“Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dressed yourself?”), his masculinity (“When you durst do it, then you were a man”) and his consistency. She also supplies the practical plan: the grooms will be made drunk and blamed.

head: Technique
Example
Effect on Macbeth and on the audience
rows: Rhetorical questions
“Was the hope drunk...?”
Makes him defend himself; suggests his ambition was only wine-courage
Challenge to manhood
“When you durst do it, then you were a man”
Redefines manliness as ruthlessness; Macbeth later echoes this idea
Shocking image of motherhood
She says she would have dashed out the brains of her baby while it smiled at her
Shows her willingness to be monstrous to keep a promise; an image of unnatural violence
Practical plan
“screw your courage to the sticking-place”
Turns emotion into action and gives confidence

bullets: She returns the daggers herself when Macbeth refuses (“Infirm of purpose! Give me the daggers”), showing practical courage.
She mocks his fear: “The sleeping and the dead / Are but as pictures”. Dead bodies are no more frightening than paintings.
The line “My hands are of your colour” is followed by a pun on “a heart so white”, playing on the **colour of blood** and the white of cowardice.
In 2.3 she faints when Macduff describes the murder. The audience can read it as genuine horror or as a deliberate distraction. Offering both readings is excellent AO1 practice.
Her confidence in “a little water” is **dramatic irony**: the audience will see it contradicted in 5.1.

callouts.p: This is a favourite for high marks. Use it to argue that Lady Macbeth's conscience is present from the start, so her breakdown in Act 5 is not a sudden change but the return of something she tried to suppress.

core.h: Act 2: the murder and the first crack
core.p: In 2.2 she waits while Macbeth commits the murder, and her nerves are shown by her fear that the plan has failed: “That which hath made them drunk hath made me bold”. The most important detail is her confession that she could not kill Duncan herself because “Had he not resembled / My father as he slept”. This brief moment reveals her conscience and humanises her. When Macbeth returns shaken, she takes control, saying “A little water clears us of this deed”.

bullets: She is **no longer the strategist**; the audience watches her become a hostess, then a nurse, then a witness.
“You have displaced the mirth” shows her social skill, but she cannot repair what his guilt has broken.
Her final public line at the feast, telling the guests not to stand upon “the order of your going”, ends her last public act as queen. She does not appear again until 5.1.
Her absence in Act 4 fits the idea that Macbeth has outgrown her influence and become a tyrant who needs no accomplice.

callouts.p: Many students jump from Act 2 to the sleepwalking. The Act 3 scenes show the shift in power and are important for any question about the relationship or about how Macbeth changes.

core.p: After Duncan's death, the relationship between the couple begins to shift. In 3.2 she is anxious (“Naught's had, all's spent”) and advises “What's done is done”, but Macbeth now keeps his plans secret, calling her “dearest chuck” and telling her to be “innocent of the knowledge”. He no longer needs her to give him orders. In 3.4 she manages the banquet and tries to cover his outburst at Banquo's ghost by telling the guests it is a habit he has had from his youth, then rebukes him with “Are you a man?”, the same weapon she used in 1.7. This time it fails.

bullets: **Fragments of earlier scenes** return: “Hell is murky”, the old man having “so much blood in him”, and the Thane of Fife's wife. She remembers more than the murders she took part in.
“All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”: the exotic luxury image is hopeless against the smell of blood. The adjective “little” makes her seem small and childlike.
She keeps a light by her continually: the woman who called on “thick night” is now afraid of darkness.
She says “What's done cannot be undone”, which contradicts her earlier “What's done is done” claim in 3.2 and shows the changed meaning.
The doctor says “More needs she the divine than the physician”: her illness is spiritual rather than medical, which fits Jacobean ideas of sin and conscience.

callouts.p: Prose is usually used for lower-status characters, comic scenes, madness or intimate speech. Verse usually signals nobility and order. Lady Macbeth's switch to prose reflects both her madness and the loss of her status as a controlling queen.

core.p: This scene reverses the Lady Macbeth we met in Act 1. Now she speaks in **prose**, not verse, which suggests a mind that has lost its order. She is observed by a doctor and a gentlewoman, so the audience sees her secret guilt through other people's eyes. She rubs her hands as though washing them, and the repeated “Out, damned spot!” reveals that the blood she dismissed as washable is now permanent.

bullets: Her offstage death is a **structural choice**: it avoids a sentimental scene and gives Macbeth the chance to deliver the “Tomorrow” speech.
The tension between **official verdict** (fiend-like) and **dramatic experience** (pitiable) is a good source of alternative interpretations.
Compare with Lady Macduff: both are wives who die as casualties of Macbeth's ambition, but Lady Macduff is killed for what her husband did, whereas Lady Macbeth is destroyed by her own decisions.

callouts.p: In a conclusion, link her to Shakespeare's message: the play shows that corrupting nature (through the unnatural murder of a king and the rejection of conscience) cannot bring lasting power.

core.h: Her death and what it means
core.p: We never see her death. In 5.5 Seyton says, “The queen, my lord, is dead”, and in 5.8 Malcolm reports that she took her own life “by self and violent hands”. This is deliberately underplayed: Macbeth's response (“She should have died hereafter”) shows how far he has withdrawn, and Shakespeare keeps the audience focused on his tragic isolation rather than on her end. Malcolm's label “fiend-like queen” is an official verdict, but the sleepwalking scene complicates it by showing her suffering.

bullets: The part would have been played by a **boy actor** in Shakespeare's theatre, adding a layer of irony to a character who rejects femininity.
Do not claim Shakespeare “hates women”. Argue what his portrayal suggests about power and gender, using specific evidence.

callouts.p: Avoid “Women were not equal in Jacobean times so Lady Macbeth is bad”. Link to a quotation: “unsex me here” suggests she believes that power requires abandoning womanhood.

core.p: Contextual links should explain why Shakespeare made her the way he did and how a Jacobean audience may have responded. Different readings are fair as long as they rely on the text.

head: Lens
What it says about Lady Macbeth
Evidence
rows: Jacobean gender roles
A woman who seeks power outside the domestic sphere upsets the order; she is punished by madness and death
“unsex me here”; her death is offstage and condemned as “fiend-like”
Witchcraft and the supernatural
Her invocation of spirits links her with the witches and suggests she is not wholly innocent or natural
“you murdering ministers”; “Come, thick night”
Hospitality and duty
She breaks the host's sacred duty to guests, a serious crime in the period
1.7: her plan to kill Duncan in her own house
Modern feminist reading
She uses the only route to power available to her, through her husband, and is destroyed by a world that gave her no legitimate outlet
“Was the hope drunk”: she must act through him
Psychological reading
Her guilt is delayed, not absent; suppression leads to breakdown
The father detail; sleepwalking

bullets: **Start with a thesis** about her role: for example: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a figure whose strength is a mask, and whose breakdown exposes the conscience she tried to unsex.
**Choose five moments**: invocation (1.5), persuasion (1.7), after the murder (2.2), the banquet (3.4), sleepwalking (5.1).
**Use language terms precisely**: imperative, rhetorical question, metaphor, antithesis, juxtaposition, prose versus verse, dramatic irony.
**Always compare early and late**: for example “A little water” (2.2) with “All the perfumes of Arabia” (5.1).
**Close with purpose**: what does Shakespeare want us to think about ambition, gender or guilt?

callouts.p: You can often earn a context mark with one embedded clause, for example: Jacobean audiences, who saw the monarch as God's deputy, would find her call to 'unsex' herself especially sinister because it threatens both gender and divine order.

core.h: Exam technique: writing about Lady Macbeth
core.p: Questions may ask about her ambition, her power, her relationship with Macbeth, or how she changes. In part (a) you will usually get an extract from 1.5, 1.7, 2.2, 3.4 or 5.1; in part (b) you must recall quotations from elsewhere. Prepare a short bank for each key scene so you can embed them smoothly.

plan: Invocation in 1.5: a woman choosing to unsex herself
Persuasion in 1.7: manhood as a weapon
2.2: the father detail reveals her conscience
5.1: the return of the repressed and the offstage death
essays.q: How does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth as a powerful but ultimately vulnerable character? (Part (b) style)
essays.text:
From her first appearance, Lady Macbeth is presented as the character who turns thought into action. In 1.5 she asks the spirits to “unsex me here”, and the imperative shows her commanding rather than begging the supernatural. The verb “unsex” implies that womanhood is a removable layer, a belief that suggests she thinks power belongs to men and must be borrowed. For a Jacobean audience, whose society expected women to remain in the domestic sphere, this invocation would be shocking, but it also reveals her ambition: she is a woman who sees no legitimate route to power and so chooses a monstrous one.

In 1.7 Shakespeare shows how her power operates through language. When Macbeth wishes to “proceed no further”, she asks “Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dressed yourself?”, a rhetorical question that turns his own ambition into a drunken fantasy. The clothing metaphor links to the play's recurring concern with borrowed robes and false appearances, so her mockery implies that his courage is a costume that she can strip away. She then redefines masculinity as ruthlessness, “When you durst do it, then you were a man”. The success of the argument shows her power, but it also shows her limits: she cannot persuade him by moral reasoning, only by making him ashamed.

Yet Shakespeare complicates her image at the moment of the murder. In 2.2 she confesses that she could not kill Duncan because “he resembled / My father as he slept”. The enjambment lets the line hang in the air for a moment, and the word “father” brings family and conscience into the scene. She is not as hard as she demanded to be. The same scene gives her the line “A little water clears us of this deed”, whose simple monosyllables underestimate the weight of guilt. The audience, with the knowledge of what is to come, hears the dramatic irony.

The power balance begins to move in Act 3. In 3.4 she tries to manage the banquet and rebukes Macbeth with “Are you a man?”, but the question that once worked now fails, and she must send the guests away. Her loss of influence is also structural: she is absent in Act 4 as Macbeth acts without consultation. Shakespeare suggests that the tyrant no longer needs a partner and that the relationship has been hollowed out by secrecy (“dearest chuck”).

In 5.1 her vulnerability is complete. She speaks in prose, not the verse of a queen, and the repeated “Out, damned spot!” shows that she is trying to order an imaginary stain. The perfumes of Arabia, symbols of wealth and luxury, cannot sweeten her “little hand”: the adjective makes her seem like a child, reducing the commanding queen to a frightened figure. A modern audience may pity her, while a Jacobean audience may see divine justice, a reading supported by the doctor's remark that she needs the “divine” more than the physician. Malcolm's description of her as “fiend-like” is the official verdict, but Shakespeare has already given us the evidence to resist it. Ultimately, Lady Macbeth embodies the play's warning that a mind cannot be unsexed or unburdened by will alone.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth's power as a performance that requires her to suppress her own conscience; the sleepwalking scene exposes the cost of that suppression, suggesting that the unnatural reordering of nature, gender and morality cannot be sustained.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis about performance and conscience controls the argument; quotations are short and embedded.
AO2: individual words (“unsex”, “dressed”, “little”) are explored; structure is considered (enjambment, absence in Act 4, prose in 5.1).
AO3: context (gender expectations, divine justice, hospitality) shapes the argument instead of being added at the end.
Offers a balanced evaluation of different audience responses and links back to the writer's purpose.

model: Soliloquy form shows her private ambition
Imperatives (“come”, “take”) show her commanding spirits
“Unsex me here”: rejects womanhood and compassion
“Take my milk for gall” turns nurture into poison
Darkness imagery (“thick night”) links to concealment and sin
Dramatic irony: Duncan is about to arrive
Context: Jacobean views of gender and the supernatural
exam.q: Starting with this speech (Act 1 Scene 5, “The raven himself is hoarse”), explain how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman. (Part (a) style; check the marks on your paper, around 20.)
exam.tip: Keep your focus on the extract. Zoom in on one or two words in detail and avoid retelling the plot.

model: Partnership in 1.5 and 1.7: she is the persuader
2.2: practical control after murder; he is shaken
3.2: Macbeth keeps her out (“dearest chuck”)
3.4: “Are you a man?” no longer works
Act 5: she is alone in her guilt; his response to her death is numb
Pattern: reversal of roles shows corrosive effect of ambition
Context: marriage and gender expectations
exam.q: Explain the importance of the relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth in the play. Refer to the whole play. (Part (b) style)
exam.tip: Track change over time and use short quotations; the best answers see the relationship as a structural pattern.

model: Prose suggests fragmentation and madness
Repetition of “Out, damned spot!” shows obsessive guilt
Image of hands and blood links to earlier “A little water”
“All the perfumes of Arabia” shows hopelessness; “little” suggests vulnerability
Light by her: fear of darkness
Doctor's remark about the divine: sin not sickness
exam.q: How does Shakespeare use language to show Lady Macbeth's guilt in the sleepwalking scene (Act 5 Scene 1)? (Part (a) style)
exam.tip: The best answers compare this scene with 1.5 and 2.2 to show reversal.

model: She questions his courage: “Was the hope drunk”
She challenges his manhood: “When you durst do it, then you were a man”
She gives a practical plan (the grooms)
She uses a shocking image about her baby to show determination
exam.q: Give two examples of how Lady Macbeth persuades Macbeth to kill Duncan. (4 marks)
exam.tip: Each point needs a quotation or a precise reference plus a short comment about the effect.

model: She sees the shortcut and invokes evil in 1.5
He admits to “vaulting ambition”, so his ambition is real
She cannot kill Duncan (“resembled my father”), showing less ruthlessness
Macbeth continues to kill alone after Act 3
Her ambition is through him, shaped by gender limits
Conclusion: she starts it, but he finishes it; his ambition proves more durable
exam.q: “Lady Macbeth is more ambitious than Macbeth.” How far do you agree? (Part (b) style)
exam.tip: State a clear stance. Compare their ambitions rather than describing each in isolation.

model: She says that she could not kill Duncan because he resembled her father
Her guilt in the sleepwalking scene shows her conscience
Her fainting in 2.3 may show real shock
exam.q: Explain one way in which Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a human being and not just a villain. (2 marks)
exam.tip: A short clear point with a quotation or a reference earns both marks.

mistakes.r: Use the father detail and the sleepwalking scene to show conscience that she suppresses early and which returns later.
mistakes.w: Saying Lady Macbeth is purely evil and has no conscience.

mistakes.r: Specify how: imperative verbs, rhetorical questions, practical planning, and then show the cost of that strength.
mistakes.w: Writing “Lady Macbeth is a strong woman” without evidence.

mistakes.r: Argue that she persuades and manipulates, but that Macbeth's ambition and free will remain; he admits he has only “vaulting ambition” himself.
mistakes.w: Claiming she forces Macbeth to kill Duncan.

mistakes.r: Use “dearest chuck” and “Are you a man?” failing to show how the relationship changes.
mistakes.w: Ignoring Act 3 and the shift of power.

mistakes.r: Tie specific beliefs (gender roles, witchcraft, hospitality) to specific quotations and say what the audience may feel.
mistakes.w: Context as a generic statement: “Women were weak in Jacobean times”.

mistakes.r: Pick two or three short phrases and analyse single words, such as “unsex” or “gall”.
mistakes.w: Quoting a long section from the 1.5 speech.

mistakes.r: Link to Jacobean ideas of guilt and sin, the use of prose, the doctor's remark about the divine, and the reversal of earlier statements.
mistakes.w: Reading the sleepwalking scene only as madness.

quotes.a: The verb “unsex” suggests removing something fixed in nature, so she believes womanhood and pity are obstacles to power. The imperative and the word “here” show her expecting immediate obedience from the spirits. The phrase also presents her as choosing evil rather than being driven to it.
quotes.c: In Jacobean England women had limited public authority, so she has to reject womanhood in order to act. A Jacobean audience would find the invocation sinister.

quotes.a: She uses “milk” as a symbol of nurture and compassion, and she judges Macbeth as too soft to take the shortcut to the crown. The phrase is ironic since she later wants her own milk turned to “gall”, so the image of nurture is turned inside out.
quotes.c: Milk links to ideas of motherhood and nature, which she tries to reject.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, early in the scene

quotes.a: Her advice to look like an “innocent flower” but be the “serpent” evokes Eden and the idea of evil hiding in a lovely form. It teaches Macbeth to be a hypocrite, and it also describes her own concealed intentions towards Duncan.
quotes.c: The serpent in Genesis would be familiar to a Christian audience as the symbol of the devil.

quotes.a: The rhetorical question accuses Macbeth of having had only borrowed courage. The metaphor of “hope” being “drunk” makes his earlier ambition seem foolish and unreliable. It is a clever attack because it turns his own loyalty to his plan against him.
quotes.c: Her use of manhood as a weapon draws on social expectations that men should be bold in action.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 7, middle of the scene

quotes.a: The mechanical metaphor of tightening a screw or a bowstring shows courage as something that can be engineered. The plosive “c” and “st” sounds add force. The line assumes that failure is only a matter of will, which she later finds untrue.
quotes.c: The image likely relates to tightening a crossbow or a musical instrument string, which suggests that the audience understood a practical comparison.
quotes.q: screw your courage to the sticking-place
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 7, late in the scene

quotes.a: This humanising detail shows she could not kill Duncan herself. The word “resembled” brings her own family into the scene and hints at a conscience that her earlier speeches tried to deny. It also suggests that her ruthlessness is partly performance.
quotes.c: Respect for fathers and kings was linked in a society where the king was the “father” of the nation.
quotes.q: Had he not resembled / My father as he slept
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 2, early in the scene

quotes.a: The simple vocabulary and the word “little” show her downplaying the crime. The line is full of dramatic irony as in Act 5 she cannot wash her hands clean. The claim contrasts with Macbeth's grand fear that the whole ocean could not cleanse him.
quotes.c: Washing and cleansing carried religious meaning of forgiveness, which she dismisses too easily.
quotes.q: A little water clears us of this deed
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 2, late in the scene

quotes.a: She repeats the challenge she used in 1.7, but now in an aside to him it sounds desperate. The question no longer persuades because the ghost has made him see the cost of his deeds. The failure of her strongest weapon shows how much has changed.
quotes.c: The play keeps questioning what “manhood” means: courage, ruthlessness or humanity.
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 4, during the ghost scene

quotes.a: The command and the exclamation show that she is still trying to control events, but this time she is ordering an imaginary stain. The word “damned” is a religious term, hinting that she is afraid of damnation. The fragmentary prose displays her broken mind.
quotes.c: Guilt and damnation were serious Jacobean concerns, supporting the doctor's remark that she needs the divine.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 1, middle of the scene

quotes.a: The luxury of “Arabia” suggests the most precious scents imaginable, yet they are useless against guilt. The adjective “little” reduces her hand to something childlike and vulnerable. The image completes the reversal from “a little water” to hopeless guilt.
quotes.c: Arabia stood for exotic luxury to the Jacobeans, an effective contrast with the squalor of guilt.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 1, late in the scene

quotes.a: Malcolm's official verdict reduces her to a monster, but the audience has seen her suffering, so his label feels too simple. The line helps establish the new regime's version of events, and it tests whether the audience agrees.
quotes.c: A ruler writing history is a political act; Malcolm needs a clear villain to restore order.

summary: Understand how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as an ambitious, manipulative and ultimately tormented figure, and how her role as persuader, partner and casualty of guilt links to gender, power, conscience and the Jacobean context.

terms.d: A calling on spirits or forces for help; Lady Macbeth's speech in 1.5 is an invocation to evil spirits.
A verb form that gives a command, such as “come”, “take” or “pour” in her 1.5 soliloquy.
A character whose qualities contrast with another to highlight their traits.
Ordinary written or spoken language without metrical structure; here a sign of fragmentation and madness.
When the audience understands the full significance of words that a character does not, e.g. “A little water clears us of this deed”.
Placing two contrasting ideas or images side by side, such as milk and gall.
A recurring image or idea (blood, hands, sleep, darkness) which builds a theme.
Excessive pride or self-confidence that leads to a fall.
Social expectations about how men and women should behave; central to her demand to be “unsexed”.
